articles.title: Why are MPs voting on assisted dying again?
articles.summary: A Labour MP has brought forward an identical bill to the previous attempt, saying she wants peers to "finish the job".
articles.body:
MPs will vote again on proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales on Friday.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would allow adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life.

This would be subject to certain safeguards, including requiring the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

Why are assisted dying proposals back in the Commons again?

Labour MP Lauren Edwards, who has brought forward an identical bill to the previous attempt, says she wants to ask the House of Lords to "finish the job".

Proposals tabled by Labour's Kim Leadbeater in 2024 to legalise assisted dying cleared the House of Commons on 20 June last year with a majority of 23.

But it did not clear all its stages in the Lords, with peers tabling more than 1,200 amendments.

Supporters of the bill accused some peers of using delaying tactics to block the proposals, while critics argued it did not have sufficient safeguards to protect vulnerable people.

From 09:30 BST, what is known as a second reading debate will take place - which gives MPs the opportunity to discuss the main principles of the bill.

The debate cannot run beyond 14:30 BST, and a vote is expected before that cut-off time.

Both sides expect the result to be close. "It's on a knife edge," one of those closely involved told the BBC.

Opponents believe support for the bill has weakened since MPs last considered it. But they are not confident they have the numbers to win the vote.

Supporters and those opposed believe the outcome will come down to who turns up on Friday, a day when many MPs are typically in their constituencies rather than in Westminster.

Several MPs the BBC spoke to despaired that such a significant social change could hinge on their colleagues' diary commitments.

"I can't tell someone not to go to their sister's wedding," said one MP leading efforts to persuade backers of the bill to vote.

Others have been convincing MPs on a planned trip to Ukraine to change their flights in order to be present.

In 2024, more than 160 MPs indicated they wanted to speak during the second reading debate on Leadbeater's bill but fewer have asked to speak this time.

Edwards made clear from the start that she wanted to bring forward a bill that was identical to the one approved by the Commons in June last year.

This paves the way for rarely used powers to override objections from peers should they refuse to pass it again.

Bills usually only become law if both Houses of Parliament agree on its final wording.

Under the terms of the Parliament Acts , if an identical bill passes the Commons in two successive parliamentary sessions then the Lords cannot halt its progress a second time.

Peers can suggest amendments which, if agreed by the Commons, would be added to the bill.

But ultimately the powers could enable the bill to become law at the end of this current session even without peers' approval.

The Parliament Acts were last used in 2004 to push through a ban on fox hunting.

Opponents have warned that using this procedure would risk creating a law which disability charities, hospices and others have raised major concerns.

Gareth Snell, a Labour MP who backed the bill last time, has signed a letter to Labour MPs saying he had "a profound concern" at the possibility of using the Parliament Acts.

"This is an extraordinary risk for us to take," he said in a letter co-signed with Dame Meg Hillier, a prominent opponent of assisted dying.

Edwards argues she does not want to use the Parliament Acts but MPs passing an identical bill would force peers to scrutinise, rather than block, the legislation.

If the bill is backed by MPs on Friday then it will proceed to the next stage known as committee, which will see possible amendments debated by MPs. However those behind the bill have made clear they would oppose any amendments suggested by MPs in order for the Parliament Acts to be in force.

Instead they would leave it to peers to suggest potential amendments.

If MPs vote against the bill on Friday, it would fall.

However supporters say even if the bill does not pass, there will be another attempt to legalise assisted dying as soon as possible.

"Whatever happens on Friday this isn't the end of assisted dying," one said. "It will come back again and again and again."

Privately they acknowledge the current makeup of Parliament, with such a large proportion of Labour MPs who tend to support assisted dying, is a "unique moment" to pass this change.

What has Andy Burnham said on assisted dying?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will not vote on the bill on Friday, noting he has his "own personal views on the issue" but it was "a matter for Parliament to decide".

Writing to Labour MPs last month , Burnham said: "My role, as the prime minister, will be to lead a government that implements the will of Parliament in this area – whether that is to change the law or not."

He also stressed the government would officially remain neutral on the bill.

In July, Burnham said the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed" before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales.

It was the first time he set out his position on the issue after becoming PM.

During his first stint as an MP, Burnham abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

In 2024, when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour" of Leadbeater's bill if he was in Parliament.

He said he had had "family experience in the nine years since that has changed my view".

Burnham caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying and insisted he would want a requirement before any new law was implemented that hospices would be "properly funded and sorted out".

articles.title: In 1976, Japan gave Seattle 1,000 cherry trees; 50 years later, the gift had grown into a cultural festival
articles.summary: Rest of World News: For Seattle, the arrival of spring carries a history that reaches back half a century. In 1976, 1,000 cherry trees arrived from Japan at a time when t.
articles.body: For Seattle, the arrival of spring carries a history that reaches back half a century. In 1976, 1,000 cherry trees arrived from Japan at a time when the United States was preparing to mark its bicentennial. The gift was presented by Japan’s former prime minister Takeo Miki as a gesture recognising the ties between Japan and Washington state. That same day, people gathered at Seward Park for a small celebration beneath the trees, with traditional music, dancing and picnic lunches on the grass. What began as a modest afternoon gathering would eventually become a major annual festival, linking cherry blossoms with a lasting cultural exchange between Japan and the Pacific Northwest.Japan’s 1,000-tree gift to Seattle began a festival tradition in 1976According to the official website Seattle Cherry Blossom & Japanese Cultural Festival, on May 8, 1976, Japan's former prime minister Takeo Miki presented Seattle with 1,000 cherry trees. The gift marked America's bicentennial and recognised the longstanding ties between Japan and Washington state.The trees also provided the starting point for a public celebration. That afternoon, the first festival was held on the grass at Seattle's Seward Park. People brought sack lunches and gathered to watch traditional Japanese music and dance on a temporary stage.The setting was simple. There was no expectation that the occasion would eventually become one of the region's longest-running Japanese cultural festivals.Cherry blossom viewing, or hanami, was part of the cultural connection from the beginning. The falling petals offered a natural setting for a gathering centred on Japanese culture, while the trees themselves became a visible reminder of the relationship between the two places.What began in Seward Park grew into a major cultural eventThe festival did not remain at Seward Park for long. In 1978, it moved to Seattle Center, where it has continued as part of the site's Festál programme.The change gave the event room to grow. What had started as an afternoon gathering developed into a three-day celebration featuring performances, demonstrations, exhibitions, workshops and community organisations.The festival has retained one feature from its early years that remains important to its identity: admission is free. Its purpose is not limited to celebrating the arrival of spring. The programme is intended to introduce visitors to Japanese arts, traditions, history and contemporary cultural life while encouraging connections between Japanese and Pacific Northwest communities.By 2026, the festival was marking its 50th anniversary. Its theme for the year was "Sakura Monogatari – Stories Beneath the Blossoms", looking back at the event's beginnings while pointing towards its next half-century.A three-day programme brings Japanese culture to Seattle CenterThe anniversary programme at Seattle Center runs from April 10 to April 12, with activities scheduled from 11am to 5pm each day.Taiko performances, martial arts, traditional music and other demonstrations form much of the public programme. More than 25 performances and hands-on activities are planned for the anniversary festival, alongside more than 35 exhibitors.As reported by Japanese Cultural & Community Center of Washington Seattle, an exhibition brings together more than 120 works by over 30 local artists, adding another layer to an event that has expanded well beyond its original music and dance performances.The festival's organisers have also brought together groups representing different forms of Japanese cultural practice in the Pacific Northwest. The result is a programme that includes both established traditions and activities shaped by Japanese American and local communities.Sumo, Okinawan crafts and taiko add new dimensions to the 2026 festivalAmong the more unusual additions to the 2026 programme is the Rain City Open, a sumo tournament taking place on Saturday morning. Around 60 competitors from across the United States are expected to take part, with men's and women's divisions.The weekend also includes opportunities to learn directly from visiting artists from Okinawa. Members of the Asato family from Asato Bingata Studio are leading workshops in bingata, a traditional Okinawan textile dyeing method recognised for its elaborate patterns and vivid colours. Participants can make small dyed objects such as bags or coasters and take them home.These activities sit alongside the better-known festival sounds. Taiko groups will perform throughout the weekend, while martial arts demonstrations and traditional music help connect the modern event with the cultural traditions that have been presented since its early years.From a 1976 gift of trees to a 50-year cultural traditionThe cherry blossom celebration now forms part of Seattle Center Festál, a year-round programme of free cultural festivals.Festál brings together 25 community-produced festivals representing different cultural traditions across the Seattle and Pacific Northwest region. Collectively, the programme records about 400,000 visits each year and generates an estimated $30 million in economic activity, according to Seattle Center.That wider setting has given the cherry blossom festival a place within a much broader calendar of cultural events. Yet its origins remain unusually specific: a diplomatic gift of trees in 1976, followed by a small gathering in a Seattle park.The anniversary therefore marks two things at once. It is 50 years since the first festival, but it also traces half a century of public cultural exchange that began with a gift intended to commemorate friendship.How a 1976 tree gift grew into Seattle’s 50-year cultural celebrationCherry trees are now a familiar part of Seattle's spring landscape, making it easy to overlook the particular history behind some of them.The 1976 gift came during the United States bicentennial, when the gesture carried both a cultural and diplomatic meaning. The festival that grew from it has kept that connection at its centre, using the blossoms as an entry point into Japanese culture rather than treating them simply as a seasonal attraction.Over five decades, the scale has changed dramatically. The first gathering involved people sitting on grass with lunches while performers used a temporary stage. The 2026 anniversary includes artists, community groups, workshops, exhibitions, a national sumo competition and performances across Seattle Center.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: IndiGo Lucknow-Dammam flight makes emergency landing in Ahmedabad after hoax bomb threat
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Lucknow to Dammam made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad airport on Thursday after a bomb threat was reported onboard.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An IndiGo flight from Lucknow to Dammam made an emergency landing at Ahmedabad airport on Thursday after a bomb threat was reported onboard, news agency ANI reported quoting Ahmedabad Police .The threat was discovered after a crew member found the word 'Bomb' written on a piece of paper inside the aircraft.There were 107 passengers and six crew members onboard the Lucknow-Dammam 6E 97 flight. All passengers and crew members were safe at Terminal 2 of the airport, police said.Ahmedabad Police said, "Lucknow-Dammam 6E 97 IndiGo flight made an emergency landing in Ahmedabad after a bomb threat onboard. A member of the crew had found 'Bomb' written on a piece of paper. There are 107 passengers and 6 crew membes onboard, all of them are safe at Terminal 2 of the airport. SOG, local Police and CISF conducted an inspection of the aircraft. Nothing suspicious was found onboard the aircraft."The Special Operations Group (SOG), local police and Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) conducted a thorough inspection of the aircraft after it landed.No suspicious object or material was found onboard during the inspection, according to the police.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Wrong turn, DHS: My name is 'Singh' and I’m not a bad truck driver
articles.summary: US News: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Trump administration’s homeland security image targeting the generic “Mr Singh” has struck a particularly sensi.
articles.body: TOI correspondent from Washington: The Trump administration’s homeland security image targeting the generic “Mr Singh” has struck a particularly sensitive nerve in the Sikh community, whose members have become a highly visible presence in American trucking, business, and indeed in public life. However, the post was later deleted.There are no federal statistics identifying truck drivers by religion, but the North American Punjabi Trucking Association (NAPTA) estimates that Sikhs account for roughly 20% of US truck drivers and about 40% on the West Coast, putting the number of Sikh truckers nationally at about 150,000.The community’s influence extends beyond driving. Many early drivers became owner-operators and eventually fleet owners. NAPTA says its membership includes about 1,400 companies operating more than 9,000 trucks, while industry estimates have put the share of US trucking companies controlled by Punjabi/Sikh operators as high as 20%. The figures are estimates, not government census data, but underscore the scale of the community’s entrepreneurial network.Also read: ‘Get off our roads, Mr Singh,’ US homeland security poster ignites backlash over targeting of SikhsTrucking offered many immigrants a relatively accessible path from employee to business owner: a driver could accumulate capital, buy a truck and eventually build a fleet. The industry also generally accommodated Sikh articles of faith, including turbans and uncut hair. Established Punjabi networks, family businesses and a shortage of American truck drivers helped fuel the community’s expansion.Its presence is visible along the nation’s freight corridors. At Exit 360 on Interstate 80 in Nebraska, for example, the Akal Travel Center, or dhaba, has become a familiar marker of the Punjabi-American trucking ecosystem.The history of Sikhs in America also complicates any portrayal of “Singh” as synonymous with a foreign newcomer. UC Davis’ Punjabi and Sikh Diaspora Digital Archive records four Sikh men arriving in San Francisco on April 6, 1899, in the first documented record of South Asian pioneers in California. Early Punjabi migrants worked in agriculture, lumber and railroads and quickly established communities across the West.They also encountered hostility. In 1907, white residents attacked South Asian workers, mainly Sikhs, in Bellingham, Washington, amid broader anti-Asian agitation. UC Davis records several such attacks and notes that most of the early South Asian pioneers were Sikhs, some of whom predated the arrival of Europeans on the east coast.For Sikh-Americans whose families have been in the country for generations, the DHS image therefore raises concerns that a surname is being used as shorthand for an entire community, blurring distinctions among citizens, permanent residents, legal immigrants and people in the country unlawfully.Ranjeev Singh Puri, a Michigan Democrat, said Wednesday that the post had particularly personal resonance. “As a proud Sikh-American, my middle name is Singh. So are my sons’. It is not a punchline, it is a surname carried proudly by millions of Sikhs worldwide, generations of whom have served this nation, built businesses, and strengthened the fabric of our democracy,” Puri said, calling the DHS post “xenophobia dressed up as public policy.”The controversy also puts a spotlight on prominent Sikh Republicans. Harmeet Dhillon, who serves as Assistant Attorney General for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division, and Nikki Haley, the former South Carolina governor and former US ambassador to the United Nations, had not publicly commented on the matter at the time of writing.Sikh-American political and civic visibility extends well beyond trucking. In 2004, Chirinjeev Kathuria became the first Indian-American to run for the US Senate while wearing a turban. Other prominent Sikh-Americans include World Bank President Ajay Banga and former US Attorney for the Southern District of New York Preet Bharara, neither of whom carries the Singh surname.For Sikh community veterans, debates over immigration enforcement, commercial driver’s licenses, English proficiency, licensing fraud and highway safety are legitimate. But they say the argument changes when a federal agency turns a surname shared by millions of people into a symbol of incompetence. For a community that has spent more than a century establishing itself on American roads, farms, businesses and institutions, that distinction matters.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Peterborough museum's prehistoric collection awarded new status
articles.summary: The exhibits span thousands of years of human history, bringing to life prehistoric artefacts.
articles.body:
A unique hoard of artefacts depicting prehistoric life has received one of the highest honours available to museums in England.

The Peterborough Museum and Art Gallery's prehistoric exhibits were among nine collections recently awarded designated status by Arts Council England.

The collection spans thousands of years, including tools and artefacts, such as Bronze Age log boats and finds from Must Farm near Whittlesey - the settlement often compared with Pompeii.

Sarah Wilson, a heritage manager at Peterborough Museum and Art Gallery, called it a "landmark moment" for the museum and the city.

"This award is a source of immense civic pride and strengthens our ability to share this remarkable heritage with residents, schools, researchers and visitors."

The designation scheme, established in 1997, highlights outstanding collections of national and international importance across England. The designation panel at Arts Council England made its decision at its most recent meeting - which is held twice a year.

Durham Cathedral's archive of a medieval monastery and the University of Liverpool's science fiction collections were among the exhibits recognised.

Darren Henley, chief executive of Arts Council England, said Peterborough museum showcased "remarkably preserved objects that represent the continuous human occupation" of the city.

Andrew Pakes, the city's Labour MP, said it was a "proud day" for the museum.

articles.title: Iran-backed Houthis seize key Red Sea port in blow to Saudi forces
articles.summary: Middle East News: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants have seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha and advanced towards the Hanish islands, bringing them closer to the B.
articles.body: Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants have seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha and advanced towards the Hanish islands, bringing them closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and raising the prospect of a major new threat to one of the world's most vital shipping routes.The rapid advance has brought the Houthis closer to the narrow maritime gateway linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, potentially giving the group greater leverage over a route critical to global oil and commodity supplies.Houthi forces have pushed Saudi-backed government troops south towards Dhubab, directly opposite Perim island at the entrance to the strait, according to two Yemeni government sources. Control of the area could put the Houthis in a position to threaten maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb.The development marks a potentially significant escalation in Yemen's long-running conflict, with fighting spreading along the country's western coastline and raising fears that the battle could spill directly into one of the world's busiest maritime corridors.The stakes extend well beyond Yemen. Any serious disruption to shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb could further strain global energy and commodity markets already facing disruption elsewhere in the region, with Brent crude trading above $100 a barrel on Thursday.Two Yemeni government sources said the Houthis had reached the Hanish islands after launching attacks that pushed government forces and their allies towards Dhubab. The town sits directly opposite Perim island, a strategically important position controlling access to the strait."Control of Dhubab and the island is key to gaining hold of the strait, they said."The fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces has intensified in recent days, with the militant group shifting its focus towards controlling Yemen's long western coastline rather than concentrating primarily on the north.Houthis deny threat to shippingDespite the advance, Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said navigation and international trade through the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb remained safe and regular.In a post on X, Abdulsalam said Yemen posed no threat to shipping and described the group's operations as defensive and limited to previously announced targets. He said the operations would end if attacks on Yemen stopped and the blockade was lifted, according to Reuters.The Houthis have previously demonstrated their ability to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea. The group launched attacks on vessels in 2023, saying it was acting in support of Palestinians during Israel's war in Gaza.Those attacks, along with strikes against Saudi Arabia, resumed this year in response to the United States' war on the Houthis' close ally Iran.The group has also declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, raising concerns that its growing position along the western coast could further threaten the kingdom's oil shipments to Asia.Why Bab el-Mandeb mattersThe Bab el-Mandeb, meaning "Gate of Tears", is the southern outlet of the Red Sea, separating Yemen from Djibouti and Eritrea. It links the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean.It is a crucial route for crude oil and fuel travelling from the Gulf towards the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, as well as commodities bound for Asia, including Russian oil.Houthi control of or increased access to positions around the strait could therefore have consequences far beyond Yemen, particularly if attacks or restrictions force commercial vessels to avoid the route.The Houthis earlier seized the historic port city of Mokha, four Yemeni government military sources said. The port is around 50 miles (80 km) from the Bab el-Mandeb.Mokha had long been held by forces aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. Its capture represents a major setback for Saudi-backed forces and gives the Houthis a stronger position along the country's western coastline.Saudi Arabia warns IranThe latest escalation has also drawn a warning from Saudi Arabia to Iran, with Pakistan delivering a message to Tehran urging it to rein in its Houthi allies after attacks on the kingdom intensified, according to Saudi, Pakistani and Iranian sources.A senior Iranian official confirmed that Pakistan conveyed the message on Tuesday. Iran's response was that "Iran does not control the Houthis".However, two Iranian sources said Tehran had told the Houthis last week to carry out attacks on Saudi Arabia, promising additional funding and weapons. They also said several Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commanders had travelled to Yemen to help coordinate the attacks.The claims could not be independently verified by Reuters.A military leader allied with Yemen's government forces said on Thursday that he had ordered his group on the west coast to establish an alternative command centre in a safe location. The instructions from Tarek Saleh, nephew of assassinated Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh, were another indication that the Houthis were pushing his National Resistance Forces away from the western coast.A video verified by Reuters showed Houthi fighters celebrating advances at a security directorate building in the Hays district south of Hodeidah. The fighters, some armed with rifles and chewing qat, chanted: "Death to America, death to Israel".Attacks intensify across Saudi borderThe Houthis said on Wednesday that Saudi strikes had hit the Yemeni provinces of Al Jawf, Marib and Saada, which border Saudi Arabia, as well as Taiz in the south and Hodeidah on the Red Sea coast.Hodeidah is a Houthi stronghold and has been used as a base for the group's wider campaign against shipping in the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia did not confirm the strikes.Saudi Arabia said Houthi attacks on the kingdom in recent days had wounded 73 people, including women and children, after civilian and economic sites in the south were targeted.The escalation has effectively opened another front in the wider conflict involving Iran and Saudi Arabia, threatening to deepen pressure on regional energy and commodity supplies.Saudi Arabia has already been using its Red Sea port of Yanbu to load millions of barrels of oil a day as it seeks to avoid disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.Any further threat to the Bab el-Mandeb could complicate the kingdom's ability to move oil towards Asian markets.Fragile Yemen truce under threatThe latest Houthi advance comes after days of intense fighting with Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and threatens to further undermine a fragile truce that took effect in 2022.The UN-brokered truce largely halted years of fighting but failed to produce a lasting political settlement. The latest clashes have raised fears of a return to full-scale conflict.The Houthis seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa, in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government south towards Aden. Saudi Arabia intervened the following year at the head of an Arab coalition, citing concerns over growing Iranian influence in Yemen and instability along its border.The resulting civil war triggered one of the world's largest humanitarian crises and led to years of fighting and devastating Saudi-led airstrikes.With Iranian support, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi transformed the group from a faction of mountain fighters into a force numbering tens of thousands.The Houthis have since developed significant missile and drone capabilities, using them to attack oil facilities and critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: British actress Lesley-Anne Down traded in LA’s fires and political leanings for a life in Georgia
articles.summary: Classic British actress Lesley-Anne Down traded in Los Angeles wildfires, Hollywood’s harassment and political leanings for a life in Georgia.
articles.body: After years of living along the Pacific coast in Malibu, British actress Lesley-Anne Down named California’s continuous wildfires and liberal-leaning politics as the reasons she and her family left the Golden State for a life in Georgia. Down lived in southern California for decades after crossing the pond to pursue her Hollywood dream, but became so let down by the environment there — both natural and political — that she would eventually become a Southern belle. But Down, now 72, perhaps best known for her film roles in 1976’s "The Pink Panther Strikes Again" and 1978’s "The Great Train Robbery," traded it all in for a serene life feeding the deer that frequent her residence outside Atlanta in what she described as the ultimate "suburban countryside." PALISADES VILLAGE TO RE-OPEN, MARKING NEW MILESTONE FOR FIRE-DEVASTATED COMMUNITY The actress and singer — known as one of Hollywood’s most beautiful women in the late ‘70s and ‘80s for her piercing blue eyes and striking features — was voted Britain’s Most Beautiful Teenager and had her breakthrough role in the British television series "Upstairs, Downstairs." "I have to be very honest. I cannot think of a more lovely place to have brought up our first lot of kids, you know, who are now all in their middle and late 40s," Down told Fox News Digital, reflecting on her time living in the Point Dume and Trancas areas of Malibu. "It was just lovely." Down, along with her husband, cinematographer and director Don E. FauntLeRoy, spent a lot of time in Malibu in the early ‘80s before they purchased their first house together on Point Dume. They lived there until 2020. "I remember looking out the kitchen window and, like, three riderless horses just going out for a little trot," she said, recalling the beauty of Broad Beach at that time, which she would later refer to as "Rock Beach" because of all the erosion. "But then it began to change — the people and, quite frankly, the fires. The fires got worse and worse." UNCONTAINED BRUSH FIRE IN NEVADA TRIGGERED BY HUMAN ACTIVITY; INFERNO GROWS TO 13K ACRES During the first 10 years of living there, Down recalled only one fire in which she was actually evacuated. But then, not more than two years later, another fire required all of her friends in Corral Canyon to vacate their homes. "We had a house full of fire victims, quite frankly, because who wants to sleep on a cot in Malibu High School? And we had a big house, so that was that," Down recalled, noting that her husband was often away working when the fires occurred. The Woolsey fire in 2018 was the last straw. Down remembered getting a police escort over Kanan Dume Road, which she said "looked like the moon" at that point. "And I said, I can’t take this anymore," she recalled, crediting her young son George, a typical Malibu-raised surfer dude at the time, with saving their home. KIRK CAMERON PRAISES NASHVILLE'S 'GOOD VALUES' AFTER DITCHING CALIFORNIA OVER COST OF LIVING, POLITICS Down and her husband had been talking for years about leaving the state but weren’t sure where to go. The growing frequency of California’s wildfires wasn’t the only factor; Down was also increasingly troubled by the state’s shift toward more liberal politics and policies. Earlier in her career, Down had also experienced her share of brushes with the industry’s casting couch. "We’re in this politically correct world, and you can only be one thing, and you can’t be anything else," Down said, noting that because of this "politically very, very frightening world" that we live in, the United States is rushing at light speed toward what her native Britain has become. "That’s always what’s happened, you know. America always follows suit from England, sort of, you know, eight to 10 years later," she said, making it a point to endorse fellow Brit and California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton to become the state’s next governor. "He’s such a smart man," she said. TRUMP-BACKED HILTON ADVANCES TO CALIFORNIA GOVERNOR GENERAL ELECTION "Quite frankly, I don’t think I’ve ever made any secret of where I feel and where I land politically, even though I was not where I am politically when I was young, but I am now," Down said. "So, I think that the chances of me ever working — even if I wanted to — in this industry, because of my politics, are slim to none." "God forbid, I was, you know, 35, and I wanted to work, and I needed to work. Guess what I’d have to do? I’d either have to be very brave and very poor, or I’d have to keep my trap shut and pretend that I’m something that I am not," she added. But to every rule there is an exception, and for Down, that meant taking on the role of Margaret Thatcher in the 2024 biopic "Reagan," around the same time she, her husband and their son moved to the Atlanta area. It was a place that FauntLeRoy was familiar with due to work ties and where their son George, who wanted to work in the industry, could thrive. For Down, the role in "Reagan" came out of the blue, and she described it as somewhat fortuitous because, as she put it, "COVID-19 left the pool of actresses smaller." "In all honesty, in my entire life, I never really wanted to be in this industry. Life just happened. And then I was on a roller coaster and that is what happened to me," Down said, noting that she felt very much a part of the "old school" of Hollywood and never transitioned well to what she referred to as the "new school" of actors in town. And when she attempted that transition, she wasn't happy. NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY CHRONICLES 20-YEAR JOURNEY BEHIND ‘REAGAN’ FILM "It was not professional as far as I could see," Down said, noting how radically the industry had changed. "When I did ‘Reagan,’ everything that I’m saying to you is not true. ‘Reagan’ was very much ‘old school.’ The people were old school, everybody behaved old school, the etiquette … the group you were with was really marvelous." "And so, you know, honestly and truly, if I could do a film or a job like that every so often, I’d do it, but they’re rare," she continued. The movie is returning to approximately 600 theaters for a wide re-release on Sept. 25. For now, Down continues to enjoy domesticity, her community of neighbors whom she calls "intensely wonderful," and the deer that visit her daily. "There’s one stag, and he’s not scared at all, and I have to tell him — I say, ‘Could you please stay away from me while I put the corn on the ground?’" Down explained in her distinctly polished but whimsical British tone. 'HERCULES' STAR KEVIN SORBO SAYS CALIFORNIA CAN KEEP ITS TAXES, TRAFFIC AND 'NEGATIVITY': 'I'M DONE' While she’ll reminisce about those days in the Malibu sun, what Down — who grew up poor and had a father who instilled in her the belief that "nothing is free" — doesn’t miss are the fires or the politics. She cites those "libbies" who can afford to say, "Everybody should have everything free," yet live in a society that needs the kind of money required to pay for all of those things. It’s not even that she doesn’t take the left’s side on some things. She said it’s about how polarizing it has become to even talk about differing views. "You can’t appear to be right-wing today, because if you appear to be on the right, or you have any right-wing political views whatsoever, they take that, and they twist it, and they use it to turn you, strangely enough, into some kind of Nazi, when really the reverse is true," Down explained. articles.title: Bromley stabbing: One man in critical condition as seven arrested
articles.summary: Seven people are arrested after a fight that an eyewitness says broke out near a KFC restaurant.
articles.body:
Seven people have been arrested after four men were stabbed in south-east London, the Metropolitan Police has said.

One of the men remains in a critical condition in hospital, while the other three are being treated for injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening.

Paramedics and the London Air Ambulance were called at about 14:20 BST to Bromley High Street, where one eyewitness reported seeing a man wielding a machete.

A fight is believed to have taken place near a KFC restaurant. KFC has told the BBC the attack did not happen within the premises, and would not comment on eyewitness accounts that a situation began there and spilled into the street.

An eyewitness, who did not want to be named, said: "I saw a fight breaking out at the door of KFC; people involved were partly inside and outside.

"A male in a grey tracksuit pulled out a machete and ran further into KFC holding it up in the air, at which point most people around KFC started running away, including my friend and I.

"I didn't turn around until we got to the shopping centre where I saw him running away with someone down a road."

Georgiana, the manager of Merkur Slots gambling shop, said she saw "a fight spill out" on to the High Street.

She said she became "very worried", and locked three customers inside the premises to wait for the situation to calm down.

She said the customers remained inside and that the shop was still closed.

Vinnie Guadagnino, who lives on Bromley High Street, said he saw a large emergency response with multiple police cars and about 10 officers on foot.

"Police cars kept coming, then within the next half hour there were multiple fire engines and people gathering.

"Then there was a drone overhead and helicopters and an air ambulance - so a massive emergency service response."

Bromley High Street is currently closed both ways from Ringers Road to Ethelbert Road.

Police remain at the scene and say there is not believed to be any wider threat to the public.

Peter Fortune, Conservative MP for Bromley and Biggin Hill, said on X that residents "would have safety concerns" and he would remain in contact with the police as they investigate.

Liberal Democrat councillor Graeme Casey said: "We're very grateful because, of course, one of the big problems we have in London is our police are quite thinly stretched, so to have had such a robust response in such a short space of time is really to the credit of all the blue-light services involved."

Matias Alil described the reaction on the street. He said: "It was terrible. We saw a massive commotion and something going on in KFC. It was really scary, to be honest."

Fergal Hickey added: "You can see the police out there have the situation under control, so you don't really need to be too anxious about it but it's still pretty crazy to see it when it happens."

articles.title: Pilot rescued after World War II-era plane crashes at Pennsylvania airport
articles.summary: The World War II-era plane had been airborne just nine minutes before crashing at Heritage Field Airport in Pennsylvania, causing a fuel leak on site.
articles.body: A World War II-era plane crashed while attempting to land at a Pennsylvania airport Wednesday evening, trapping the pilot inside the overturned aircraft before police and an airport employee freed him, authorities said. Limerick Township police responded to Heritage Field Airport around 7:17 p.m. and found the small aircraft upside down on the runway with the pilot, its only occupant, trapped inside. An airport employee and officers freed the pilot from his parachute and pulled him from the plane, police said. FIERY SAN DIEGO PLANE CRASH KILLS 2 "We got reports the pilot was trapped in the plane. On our arrival, they were pulling him out. So there was no extrication needed by the fire department," Limerick Township Fire Chief Ken Shuler told FOX29 Philadelphia. The pilot was conscious and able to stand but had visible cuts, police said. He was treated at the scene by Freedom Valley Medical Rescue and taken to a hospital. The pilot was transported to Reading Trauma Center and was alert and talking after the crash, according to FOX29. No further update on his condition was available. The single-engine plane had taken off from Pottstown and was headed to Quakertown, the station reported, citing Limerick Township officials. It had been in the air for about nine minutes. FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS The crash caused a fuel leak, according to the outlet, and firefighters remained at the airport to address the spill and watch for a possible fire. Heritage Field Airport, formerly Pottstown Municipal Airport, serves private and recreational aircraft. The airport remained closed Wednesday night while crews handled the fuel leak and removed the plane. Police said they notified the Federal Aviation Administration's Eastern Region Operations Center after the crash. articles.title: Meet Mateo Castillo-Bonde, the 11-year-old Minneapolis guitarist who went from playing in his bedroom to performing before thousands with Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis
articles.summary: US News: Mateo Castillo-Bonde, an 11-year-old from Minneapolis, left thousands at the State Fair Grandstand speechless, doing something most pre-teens his age .
articles.body: Mateo Castillo-Bonde, an 11-year-old from Minneapolis, left thousands at the State Fair Grandstand speechless, doing something most pre-teens his age do not. He played a guitar solo with the kind of precision that only comes from years of intensive practice. He did it in front of legendary producers Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis. Just like the audience, the musicians also forgot they were watching a kid who was figuring out the basics of guitar only a few years ago.Who is Mateo Castillo-Bonde?Mateo Castillo-Bonde is a sixth-grader at Plymouth Middle School. Like most kids his age, Mateo’s room is filled with Legos and posters of his favourite bands. He plays guitar like a professional, even though it’s only been three years since he started taking guitar seriously. “I just like them because they are guitar dudes. I don't know what I am. I'm a guitar player,” Mateo Castillo-Bonde told Fox 9.Mateo grew up admiring Michael Jackson and Prince. Three years ago, Mateo visited the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and something clicked. The museum visit wasn't meant to be transformational, but watching the histories of guitar legends sparked something in him that stuck. He returned home, picked up a guitar and decided to take it seriously. “I just started playing,” he recalled. His parents knew Mateo was serious about it, so they enrolled him in guitar lessons twice a week. “I think right away we noticed that he had an aptitude. His first recital, he played and, I mean, I was just blown away. You know, he sang, he played the guitar and it was just amazing,” Mark Bonde, Mateo's father, told the outlet.He practised for endless hours. The progression has been steep. The performances started quietly: the national anthem before a Gopher women's basketball game. Then came slots with the Purple Playground at Paisley Park, paying tribute to Prince's legacy in Prince's own studio. Each gig built confidence, muscle memory and passion.“It's just really fun to play the guitar. I feel like I can get my emotions out,” Mateo said.The State Fair stageJam and Lewis were headlining a homecoming concert, and they wanted to honour Jellybean Johnson, the guitarist who played on Janet Jackson's ‘Black Cat’ and died last year. That’s when they came to know about the ‘Minneapolis Mateo’. “I was shocked. I didn't think that they'd pick me for something like that,” Mateo said. They decided to bring the kid, and what happened after was, well, history.He played it right. Fans called it the highlight of the show. “It was crazy. It felt like all my practice led up to that moment. And it felt really, really good afterwards,” Mateo said.The 11-year-old wasn’t even super nervous when he got on the stage. And after hearing such rave reviews, Mateo is thrilled.“It seems like people liked it and, yeah, I don't really know, but Terry said that he thought that I did really well, and that I should keep playing guitar,” Mateo recalled.Mateo’s mum, Jenny Castillo, was equally moved by what has transpired. “For him to be able to get up and play in front of thousands and thousands of people like that is something that most grown people can't do. So the fact that he's 11 and he can do that is, it's pretty inspiring. He's an inspiration,” she told the outlet.Mateo has quite a few plans for the future. And surprisingly enough, the pre-teen knows that the road ahead can be both frustrating and rewarding. However, he has no plans to slow down. What's striking is how Mateo hasn't let any of this new fame go to his head.“I don't want to be super duper famous. I just want to be pretty famous. Because I feel life won't be that great if I'm super duper famous. Because a lot of people say that fame isn't good,” the kid said. It's the kind of grounded thinking that usually takes years and some hard knocks to arrive at. But he's eleven.Mateo already knows what his path forward is. “My hopes for the future are maybe to write really cool guitar riffs and share them with the world. And I hope that I inspire a younger generation to stop watching brain rot and actually do something.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis reportedly seize strategic Red Sea port of Mokha
articles.summary: Mokha's capture would bring the Iran-backed group closer to controlling the Bab al-Mandab Strait waterway, a key shipping route.
articles.body:
Yemen's Houthi movement has seized the strategic Red Sea port city of Mokha from Saudi-backed pro-government forces, military sources say.

The capture of Mokha would bring the Iran-backed group closer to controlling the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route about 75km (46 miles) to the south that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed and thousands displaced since the Houthis launched an offensive in the south-western coastal region a week ago.

At the same time, there has been a significant escalation in the Houthis' conflict with neighbouring Saudi Arabia that has contributed to a surge in global oil prices.

On Tuesday, the Houthis launched dozens of drones and missiles at southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 73 civilians and causing fires at several oil facilities that led to a temporary halt in operations, according to Saudi authorities.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for dozens of Saudi air strikes on their territory in north-western Yemen in recent days, including one on a prison in the town of Hazm in Jawf province that local officials said killed at least 23 civilians.

A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's government against the Houthis in the country's devastating civil war for more than a decade.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The Red Sea has become crucial for Saudi Arabia's oil exports since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran, which has led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title: Israel's Netanyahu to sue Haaretz over claim UAE warned him of 7 October attack
articles.summary: The paper said it stood by its reporting, after publishing extracts from a book where the claim appears.
articles.body:
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has told lawyers to begin defamation proceedings against an Israeli newspaper over reports that the leader of the United Arab Emirates warned him that Hamas was planning an operation just days before the 7 October 2023 attacks.

According to book extracts published by Haaretz, UAE President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had a phone call with Netanyahu that September.

The report said Netanyahu was warned that the then-Hamas chief in Gaza, Yahya Sinwar, was planning a major operation.

Netanyahu's office said "no warning was given to the prime minister from the United Arab Emirates before 7 October", calling the report part of a "sinister plot".

Haaretz, which has historically been a vocal critic of the prime minister, has stood by its reporting and rejected Netanyahu's defamation claim, saying its "sole purpose is to silence journalistic criticism".

The report - and Netanyahu's angry denials, accusing Haaretz of lies - comes as the general election campaign in Israel starts to heat up. The polls on 27 October are widely considered a referendum on Netanyahu's leadership.

On 7 October 2023, thousands of Hamas-led gunmen breached the Gaza border fence and attacked nearby Israeli communities, military bases and a large music festival. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken back to Gaza as hostages.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which at least 73,670 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Ever since 7 October, accusations have been laid against Netanyahu that he did not act quickly enough after the attack began. He has resisted an independent public inquiry into what happened and this latest report will only fuel critics' suspicions.

The report, published on Tuesday, cited three "foreign senior sources" and a Palestinian adviser to Sheikh Mohammed as saying that, in the final days of September 2023, a representative from the UAE embassy went to the Israeli prime minister's office with a special phone to ensure the conversation would remain confidential.

During that call, Haaretz reported, Netanyahu was given an explicit warning by Sheikh Mohammed - that Sinwar had told a former Palestinian official that Hamas was preparing a major operation that he described as an "earthquake".

"Bin Zayed expressed concern that the event in question would not only lead to bloodshed but also destabilise the entire region," Haaretz said, adding that the information contained in its report was a result of extensive research of dozens of sources, documents and correspondence, all carried out for a book, Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment, written by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval.

"To his surprise however, the prime minister reacted with relative calm," Haaretz reported. "Netanyahu said that, in his assessment, Hamas intended to operate in the West Bank area, and he reassured bin Zayed that Israel was prepared for any scenario."

The report went on to recount that the Emirati leader relayed the conversation he had with Netanyahu to the then CIA director William J Burns. It also said Netanyahu failed to brief the heads of Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency and Mossad intelligence agency, as well as the Israeli army's chief of staff about his conversation with the UAE president.

The report was published on the same day that the UK announced sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank. The decision angered the Israeli government, which announced several countermeasures, including ordering the closure of the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem.

But while that development made international headlines, it was the Haaretz story that led the news in a country getting ready for elections.

Netanyahu's Likud Party accused Haaretz of "blatant foreign interference in Israel's elections", while the prime minister said on X that the story had "clear political timing, as part of the left's election campaign".

Lawyers for Haaretz responded to Netanyahu's plans to begin legal proceedings, saying they would not be deterred by what they described as the prime minister's attempts to silence journalistic criticism.

The lawyers' letter stated that the report was "the product of an in-depth journalistic investigations and is based on sources pertaining to an issue of paramount public importance".

"In the absence of a full accountability to the public on behalf of your client, the press fulfils its role and exposes step by step the information to the public," it added.

While the UAE has not addressed the conversation specifically, it did not deny it either, issuing a statement emphasising that, since the attack by Hamas, it has worked towards de-escalation, regional stability and preventing violence.

"UAE and Israeli government entities have maintained open and direct lines of communication since the inception of the relationship more than five years ago," the UAE's ministry of foreign affairs said in a statement after the publication of Haaretz's report. "When necessary, all relevant intelligence has been and continues to be communicated between the relevant entities."

Four of Israel's main opposition leaders issued a joint statement demanding an investigation into what happened.

"Netanyahu and his partners in the 7 October government are unfit to continue in office," said Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Avigdor Lieberman and Yair Golan.

"We will work with the co-ordination and responsibility required to prevent them from leading to another disaster."

articles.title: Disabling cameras, ‘excessive invasive’ searches: 20 years on, Iran faces UN council over nuclear probe
articles.summary: Middle East News: The UN’s nuclear watchdog has asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable for its failure to comply with safeguards designed to prevent the.
articles.body: The UN’s nuclear watchdog has asked the UN Security Council to hold Iran accountable for its failure to comply with safeguards designed to prevent the development of nuclear weapons, diplomatic officials said Wednesday.It is the latest chapter in a more than decade-long effort to monitor Iran, during which the country has moved from compliance to obstructing inspection efforts. These have included disabling monitoring cameras and subjecting inspectors to “excessively invasive physical searches”, according to former officials, diplomats and more than a decade of UN documents, as cited by CNN.The board referred Iran to the Council for the first time in 20 years, citing Tehran’s failure to cooperate with a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites.Western officials suspect the traces may indicate that Iran had a secret nuclear weapons programme until 2003. Tehran has denied pursuing nuclear weapons, maintaining that its nuclear programme is entirely peaceful.Tehran was last referred to the UN Security Council in early 2006, after which the body imposed a series of measures, including sanctions, against Iran.Since February 2026, when the US and Israel launched their air campaign against Iran, the IAEA has been unable to inspect any Iranian nuclear facility except the Bushehr nuclear power plant, as cited by CNN.IAEA officials have said the inspection gap has disrupted the agency’s “continuity of knowledge” about Iran’s uranium, enrichment centrifuges and other monitored nuclear materials, leaving it unable to verify their status, quantity or location.Iran’s 2015 nuclear deal with the US and other countries established one of the world’s most extensive nuclear inspection regimes, overseen by the International Atomic Energy Agency.For years, Tehran’s nuclear programme remained compliant with inspections by the agency.But in the years after US President Donald Trump withdrew from the deal, Iran gradually and systematically breached its nuclear safeguards, according to contemporaneous IAEA reports.The agency later concluded that Tehran had failed to declare sites linked to nuclear material.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Philadelphia put white roofs on 340 low-income seniors’ homes; temperatures fell 5°F, saving 560 kWh annually in AC electricity
articles.summary: US News: Philadelphia tested a simple way to protect older, low-income residents from summer heat by putting reflective white roof coatings on hundreds of home.
articles.body: Philadelphia tested a simple way to protect older, low-income residents from summer heat by putting reflective white roof coatings on hundreds of homes between 2001 and 2003. The Cool Homes Programme targeted elderly households living in the city’s older housing stock, where dark roofs could absorb intense sunlight and transfer heat into upper-floor rooms. Around 340 low-income seniors’ homes are cited in later accounts of the project, while programme records describe a broader group of hundreds of treated households. Monitoring found that the intervention substantially reduced heat entering the homes, with maximum ceiling temperatures falling by roughly 4–5°F. A later account also reported annual air-conditioning electricity savings of about 560 kWh per home. The project combined reflective roofs with insulation and other measures to improve comfort and energy efficiency.Philadelphia’s white-roof project targeted 340 low-income seniors’ homesPhiladelphia’s older rowhouses were particularly vulnerable to summer heat because many had flat roofs covered with dark roofing materials that absorbed sunlight. Heat collected on these surfaces could pass through the roof and make upper-floor rooms uncomfortable during hot weather. The problem was especially important for older residents, who can be more vulnerable to extreme heat. The city’s Cool Homes Programme, implemented by the Energy Coordinating Agency, was designed to address this problem among low-income households while also helping reduce energy consumption. The programme did more than apply reflective coatings. Depending on the property, workers also carried out roof repairs, added insulation, installed whole-house fans and provided residents with information on managing heat inside their homes.White roofs reflected the summer heatThe principle behind the intervention was straightforward. A conventional dark roof absorbs much of the sunlight that reaches it, causing the roof surface to become extremely hot. A white or highly reflective coating sends a larger proportion of incoming solar radiation back away from the building. Combined with insulation, this reduces the amount of heat transferred into the rooms below. Temperature monitoring during the Philadelphia project showed a substantial difference. An EPA evaluation found that the treatment reduced daily maximum ceiling temperatures by about 4.7°F, while maximum room-air temperatures dropped by roughly 2°F. The study also found that the combination of reflective coating and insulation greatly reduced solar heat gain through the roof.The project also reduced air-conditioning demandThe cooling effect had an important energy consequence because residents needed less mechanical cooling to maintain comfortable indoor temperatures. A later account of the Philadelphia project reported that each treated home saved about 560 kWh of air-conditioning electricity per year. That figure is equivalent to hundreds of kilowatt-hours of electricity that otherwise would have been used to remove heat from the homes. The original programme evaluation, however, did not have sufficient post-treatment electricity-use data to independently establish the 560 kWh figure. It did report energy benefits from the broader weatherisation work, including estimated reductions in natural-gas consumption. The electricity-saving figure is therefore best presented as a later reported result of the project rather than as a direct finding of the original evaluation.It was designed as a heat-health interventionSaving electricity was only part of the reason the programme mattered. Philadelphia's Cool Homes effort was created with vulnerable residents in mind, particularly older people living in homes that could become dangerously hot during summer heat events. The programme combined physical improvements with advice on ventilation, fans, windows and other ways of coping with hot weather. By reducing the amount of heat entering upper-floor rooms, reflective roofs and insulation could improve indoor comfort even before residents switched on their air conditioners. The project therefore linked energy efficiency with heat resilience, an approach that has become increasingly relevant as cities face more frequent and intense periods of extreme heat.Philadelphia’s cool-roof idea lives onThe experiment became part of a broader shift towards reflective roofing in Philadelphia. The city adopted cool-roof requirements for certain new construction and major renovation projects in 2010, making reflective roofing part of its building-efficiency strategy. More recently, Philadelphia has continued examining cool roofs as a way to improve energy efficiency and neighbourhood heat resilience. In 2024, the city announced more than $1.3 million in federal funding for energy-efficiency and conservation projects, including a new Cool Roofs Programme developed with the Energy Coordinating Agency. The modern programme is examining how reflective roofs can be expanded in homes and communities. What began as a targeted effort for vulnerable residents more than two decades ago has therefore become part of a much larger conversation about how simple changes to buildings can help cities cope with rising heat while reducing energy demand.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: More than 20 children feared dead in DR Congo school fire
articles.summary: Officials say there was a stampede as they fled a fire that engulfed two schools in the eastern rebel-held city of Bukavu.
articles.body:
At least 24 schoolchildren are feared dead in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a senior official there has said.

Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.

Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.

Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.

Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.

A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.

Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.

Rebel‑appointed authorities say they are assessing the situation and will release a provisional death toll this evening.

Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.

"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.

"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."

The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.

In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

articles.summary: Rest of World News: Princess Diana’s iconic black “revenge dress” is set to go under the hammer in New York this December, nearly three decades after it was last sold at .
articles.body: Princess Diana’s iconic black “revenge dress” is set to go under the hammer in New York this December, nearly three decades after it was last sold at auction. The silk Christina Stambolian dress will headline Sotheby’s standalone fashion evening auction on December 9, with an estimated value of $150,000 to $300,000, or roughly Rs 1.4 crore to Rs 2.8 crore.Diana wore the off-the-shoulder, fitted black dress to a Vanity Fair party at London’s Serpentine Gallery in June 1994, the same evening a television interview with her estranged husband, then-Prince Charles, aired in which he addressed his infidelity during their marriage. Diana had owned the dress for three years but had previously considered it too daring for a public appearance.The outfit quickly became one of Diana’s most recognisable fashion moments. With its bold neckline, pearl choker and striking styling, the dress marked a more confident phase in her public image and later earned the nickname “Revenge Dress”. It has since become a lasting pop-culture reference for using fashion to make a statement after a high-profile breakup or scandal.Diana never wore the dress publicly again. In 1997, she included it among 79 dresses she put up for auction to raise funds for cancer and AIDS charities. The current owners acquired it at that sale and have kept it ever since. Part of the proceeds from the upcoming auction will benefit NHS Lothian Charity on behalf of the Royal Hospital of Edinburgh.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Pilot warned Amazon cargo plane going too fast before deadly crash, data shows
articles.summary: One pilot told the other about the aircraft's "excessive speed" but received an uneven response even as alarms sounded.
articles.body:
A pilot onboard an Amazon cargo plane that crashed in Miami, Florida, on Sunday noted it was going too fast before it overshot a runway, crashed into other vehicles and burst into flames, new flight data shows.

The investigation update from the US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said one pilot warned the other in the cockpit multiple times about "the aircraft's excessive speed" but noted "there was but not a consistent verbal response", even as an altitude alarm sounded.

The Boeing 767-300's landing speed was 158 knots (292km/h), which experts have noted was on the high end.

The NTSB is leading the investigation into the crash that killed five people and injured five more.

The flight data released by NTSB included the plane's speed, altitude, and other details like flap deployment as it approached the runway. The update also included the summary of conversation between the two pilots.

The summary noted the pilot's cautions about speed occurred "throughout the remainder of the recording" as did the inconsistent verbal response.

The update said there was an electronic "sink rate sink rate" callout during the final minutes - an automated safety warning about the speed of descent.

There was also an ​electronic "too low terrain" callout, another automated verbal warning that the plane was flying too close to the ground without being properly prepared for landing.

Aviation attorney Pablo Rojas told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, that it was difficult to know without the actual recording what the NTSB was referring to when it noted the inconsistent verbal response.

"But, it really confirms that this was, in a way, a doomed approach," he said.

Rojas noted that flap deployment data included in NTSB's update also could be an area of concern. The flaps, located on the back of the wings, are "part of what helps the plane kind of slow down and gently approach a landing", he said.

"The flap deployment here happened much later in the accident sequence," Rojas said. "That's maybe because the pilots were responding to the fact that they were going too fast."

After it overshot the runway, the plane - Amazon Prime Air Flight 7598 - struck equipment on the ground, hit a white Ford van, then continued onward through a perimeter fence.

It then collided with a Toyota Corolla, before coming to rest about 1,300ft (394m) beyond the runway.

The five who died were part of a plane-cleaning crew in the van. Miami authorities on Tuesday identified them as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47.

articles.title: More than 20 children feared dead in DR Congo school fire
articles.summary: Officials say there was a stampede as they fled a fire that engulfed two schools in the eastern rebel-held city of Bukavu.
articles.body:
At least 24 schoolchildren are feared dead in a stampede as they tried to flee a fire that engulfed two schools in rebel-held Bukavu in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a senior official there has said.

Adults are also reported to have died in the fire and there are fears that the death toll could rise further in the densely populated Kadutu commune.

Survivors have been taken to nearby hospitals, and footage of the scene shows children lying on hospital floors in pain.

Some 300 houses have also been destroyed in the fire, the cause of which is unknown.

Pictures circulating on social media show young children lying motionless on the ground.

A witness quoted by Reuters news agency said the fire had been put out by afternoon but smoke was still rising from rubble and corrugated metal.

Bukavu, the capital of South Kivu province and one of DR Congo's most crowded hillside cities, was captured by M23 rebels in February last year.

Rebel‑appointed authorities say they are assessing the situation and will release a provisional death toll this evening.

Meanwhile the government in Kinshasa released a statement on X, without specifying numbers of casualties.

"The Ministry of National Education and New Citizenship expressed deep sorrow over the deadly fire," it said.

"With several lives lost and many injured, the toll remains provisional. The minister offered condolences, affirmed solidarity with families, and ordered assessments of affected schools to ensure learning continuity."

The tragedy follows a similar fire in Kinshasa last weekend, where residents died in a stampede at a wedding banquet hall.

In response, the government has ordered strict safety measures and deployed teams nationwide to enforce standards at public gathering places.

articles.title: Esther Rantzen says she is too fragile to travel to Switzerland to end life
articles.summary: The broadcaster and campaigner says she missed her chance to go before living with cancer became "unbearable".
articles.body:
Dame Esther Rantzen has said she is now "too physically fragile" to travel to Switzerland to end her life at an assisted suicide clinic.

The veteran broadcaster, 86, said she would have to fly to the country, where the practice is legal, alone, which she could only have done before her life became "unbearable" and before she was ready to end her life.

The Childline founder, who is terminally ill with cancer, first revealed in December 2023 that she had joined the Dignitas clinic.

Dame Esther used her statement on Thursday to reiterate a plea for MPs to vote in favour of legalising assisted suicide in England and Wales when proposed legislation is revisited by Parliament on Friday.

She announced she had joined Dignitas about a year after being diagnosed with stage four lung cancer.

"Unfortunately, when I was strong enough to make the flight and go to Dignitas, my life was not unbearably painful, indeed I was able to relax in my beloved cottage in the New Forest," she said.

"And by the time life did become unbearable, I was too physically fragile to make the journey and go through the Dignitas process.

"So even though I had spent the money and made the plans, I was not ready to end my life back then, and did not realise that would be my last chance."

Dame Esther added that "everything I didn't want to happen I'm having to go through now", with loved ones either unable to visit her or "see me suffering pain or indignity" when they do.

The prominent assisted suicide campaigner said the law - which she described as "messy and cruel" - must "change and change quickly".

Helping someone end their life is currently considered a criminal offence across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

MPs are considering a draft law that, if passed, would make it legal in England and Wales under specific circumstances for people who are terminally ill with less than six months to live.

While Dame Esther, who is best known for presenting the BBC programme That's Life! for 21 years, is among several leading figures in favour of the bill, there are also campaigners against it, including Paralympian Baroness Grey-Thompson

They fear that a change in the law could mean that disabled and other vulnerable people could be pressured to end their lives, while also criticising the wording of the proposed legislation as not providing strong enough safeguards.

The bill has been through several drafts and has been scrutinised by several Parliamentary committees and the House of Lords, which submitted 1,200 amendments.

The bill was previously introduced in 2024, but the last session of Parliament ran out of time before it was passed.

It was reintroduced in this Parliament and a second vote will be held on Friday afternoon. If it passes the House of Commons, rarely invoked powers could be used , meaning it would not need the assent of the Lords to become law this time.

Proponents of the bill have indicated they would try to bring legislation again as soon as possible were it to be voted down on Friday.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not be voting on the issue and has suggested that palliative and social care should be better funded before legalising assisted suicide is considered.

Assisted suicide is legal in a number of countries - including Canada, Australia and Belgium - as well as in Switzerland, though the circumstances under which it is legal differ between those nations.

articles.body: US mortgage rates rose for the third consecutive week, pushing the average rate on a 30-year fixed home loan to its highest level in more than 14 months.The benchmark rate climbed to 6.76% from 6.71% last week, mortgage buyer Freddie Mac said on Thursday, compared with 6.35% a year ago, as cited by AP.Higher mortgage rates can add hundreds of dollars to borrowers’ monthly costs, reducing homebuyers’ purchasing power. Rising rates can also prompt prospective buyers to delay purchases, contributing to largely stagnant US home sales again this year.The average mortgage rate is now at its highest level since June 26, 2025, when it stood at 6.77%.Borrowing costs for 15-year fixed-rate mortgages, which are often used for refinancing, also increased this week. The average rate rose to 6.09% from 6.04% last week, compared with 5.5% a year ago.Mortgage rates are influenced by factors including inflation, Federal Reserve policy decisions and bond market expectations about the economy. They generally move in line with the 10-year Treasury yield, which lenders use as a benchmark for pricing home loans.Mortgage rates and bond yields have mostly risen this year amid the US war with Iran, which has pushed oil prices sharply higher.
